newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Independent TV taken off air in rural Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Independent TV taken off air in rural Serbia.

text.p: The most trusted and watched television station in Serbia went off the air in most of the country on Thursday evening amid a fierce battle for control of the media ahead of elections later this year.

State telecommunications authority PTT cut the station's transmission lines going south from Belgrade, stopping its coverage of cities south of Belgrade, Velimir Zugic, techical manager of BK Television, told Reuters on Friday.
"We are now only covering Belgrade and northern parts of Serbia -- cities like Novi Sad," he said.
"We have now been halved in coverage. That means in future, unless we find another solution we are going to be really a local station, not a national station."
According to a recent poll, BK TV was rated as the most watched and most trusted station in the country by far.
"Probably that is the reason which prompted the government to reduce our coverage in Serbia," Zugic said.
Early this month Serbian Radio Television (RTS) network warned BK TV it could no longer count on its transmitters to broadcast outside Belgrade, citing financial reasons.
BK TV saw the move as the "most flagrant attack on media freedom in Serbia and the right of citizens to be informed".
The move comes after a political upheaval in Serbia caused by election fraud last November by the ruling Socialist Party (SPS) of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

Huge demonstrations by Serbia's Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition groups, drawing up to 500,000 at their peak, forced Milosevic to restore local election victories in 14 cities, including Belgrade.
The widespread protests were the biggest-ever challenge to Milosevic's 10-year rule.

The opposition demands free access to the media which the SPS, fighting to reinstate its battered popularity ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections later this year, is loath to concede despite heavy pressure by the West.
The United States has retained an outer wall of sanctions against Belgrade barring Milosevic from desperately needed foreign capital to resuscitate his moribund economy.

Belgrade's commitment to democracy, human rights and freedom of the press, is one of the conditions for the sanctions to be lifted and the latest stifling of the media will diminsh chances of that happening in time for Milosevic to score election points.
BK TV's owner Bogoljub Karic had been one of Milosevic's closest allies but fell out with him after the November election fiasco.
Karic, whom analysts see as a potential presidential contender, criticised Milosevic for mishandling the affair.
He said he backed any force seeking to reintegrate Serbia into the world as a modern, democratic and free market society.
Milosevic's popularity has plummeted from 32 percent to 13 percent and for the first time he was trailing behind another politician in February opinion polls.
Western diplomats believe Milosevic will not even run for the presidency of Serbia but opt instead opt for the post of federal president.
